svg.text: Is this reference still valid? One compare, no dereference
Every key block gets a generation number when allocated, and key blocks are released in allocation order. The tree remembers only the generation of the last
block it released, lastReclaimedKeyGeneration. A RangeRef carries the generation of its first block, blockGen: it is valid exactly when blockGen is greater.
keyBlocks in allocation order; the pool blocks they occupy are named in grey

Why this is cheap and why it is correct
Cheap: validity is one integer compare against a single counter. Nothing in the referenced block is read, so a block that now holds a node, or a
newer key block, is never interpreted as the old key. Stale descriptors may sit in nodes until a search meets them; they are then removed or refreshed.
Correct: because key blocks are released in allocation order, every block with generation ≤ lastReclaimedKeyGeneration is gone and every block above it is
live. A record that continues into later blocks is valid while its first block is, since those later blocks cannot have been released before it.
Node generations are a separate mechanism
Key-block generations decide whether a RangeRef may be read. Node generations decide whether a deferred-cleanup record still names the node it was queued for.
On release a node’s generation is cleared, and the field lies beyond the bytes the pool’s free-list link overwrites. When the queue drains, a record whose generation no
longer matches the node is skipped: here L2 was released since it was queued. Node blocks are not released in allocation order, so one counter would not do.
